summary: Describes how to use TESLA, a scheme that lets receivers check that packets really came from the claimed sender and were not altered, in the ALC and NORM multicast content delivery protocols. It covers only authenticating the sender's packets, not those sent by receivers. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5776 describes how the ALC and NORM multicast file transfer protocols can use TESLA, a scheme that lets every receiver check that a packet really came from the sender and was not changed on the way. The sender uses one key per time interval and reveals each key only after the interval it protected has passed, so a receiver can check a packet once the key arrives.

questions: how does tesla authenticate multicast packets
what is the tesla group mac
what is a tesla key chain
subtitle: How receivers of a multicast file transfer can be sure the packets came from the sender and were not altered.

tldr.problem: In a multicast session anyone on the path can inject packets that look like the sender's, corrupting the file the receivers rebuild. A shared group key cannot be used, because any member could then impersonate the sender.
tldr.mechanism: TESLA uses a chain of keys, one per time interval, that the sender reveals one interval at a time. A receiver checks a packet against the key for its interval once that key has been revealed, which is a cheap message authentication code rather than a signature.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document covering only the packets the sender generates. The authentication of packets sent by receivers is out of its scope.

today: RFC 5776 is an Experimental document from April 2010, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It specifies only the authentication of packets generated by the session's sender, and it depends on external mechanisms for delivering the sender's public key and for time synchronization.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
Many applications using multicast and broadcast require that each receiver be able to authenticate the source of any packet it receives and the integrity of those packets. That is the case with ALC and NORM, two Content Delivery Protocols designed to transfer objects such as files reliably between a session's sender and several receivers. NORM is based on bidirectional transmissions: each receiver acknowledges data received, or asks for retransmissions where packets were erased. ALC is based on purely unidirectional transmissions, with reliability achieved by cyclic transmission of the content within a carousel or by proactive Forward Error Correction codes. Both operate at the application level on top of an erasure channel where packets can be lost during transmission.

The goal is to counter attacks where an attacker impersonates the session's sender and injects forged packets, corrupting the objects the receivers reconstruct. Preventing this is much more complex for group communication than for unicast. With unicast, a simple solution exists because the sender and receiver share a secret key with which they compute a Message Authentication Code of all messages exchanged. That is no longer feasible for multicast and broadcast, since sharing a group key between the sender and all receivers means any group member can impersonate the sender and send forged messages to other receivers.

The usual solution is to rely on asymmetric cryptography and digital signatures, but that is limited by high computational costs and high transmission overheads. TESLA is an alternative that provides the two required services while being compatible with high-rate transmissions over lossy channels.

The memo is explicit about its limits. It only considers the authentication and integrity verification of the packets generated by the session's sender, and not the packets that receivers may send, such as NORM's feedback packets. It also relies on several external mechanisms: a way to communicate the sender's public key or a certificate securely, a way to communicate the group key when the Group MAC feature is used, and secure time synchronization, either directly or through a time reference. These must be deployed alongside TESLA.
sections.plainLanguage: The threat is a fake sender injecting packets into a multicast session. Signing every packet would work but costs too much on a fast lossy link. TESLA gets the same guarantee with a cheap check, at the price of needing reasonably accurate clocks.

sections.title: The Key Chain
sections.content:
The sender computes a one-way key chain of n_c keys, where n_c is N plus 1, and assigns one key from the chain to each interval, consecutively but in reverse order. Key numbering starts at 0 and increases consecutively following the time interval numbering, giving K_0, K_1 through K_N. To compute the chain the sender first selects a Primary Key, K_N, and a pseudo random function f. The memo stresses that the randomness of the Primary Key is vital to the security and that no one should be able to guess it.

The function F is a one-way function defined as F(k) = f_k(0), the result of applying the pseudo random function to k and the value 0. The function F' is defined as F'(k) = f_k(1). The sender computes all the keys of the chain recursively, starting with K_N, using K_{i-1} = F(K_i), so that K_i equals F applied N minus i times to K_N. The receiver can therefore compute any value in the key chain from K_N alone, even without the intermediate values. The key used for the MAC computation is derived from the corresponding chain key by K'_i = F'(K_i).

The chain has a finite length, N, corresponding to a maximum duration of (N plus 1) times the interval duration. A first solution is a single chain long enough for the whole session, but the longer the chain, the more memory and computation are needed to cope with it. The alternative is to switch to a new chain of the same length when necessary, and all chains must have the same length with keys numbered consecutively following the interval numbering.

Switching chains requires a commitment to the new chain to reach the receiver securely. The memo specifies the in-band mechanism: the sender includes the commitment F(K_{N+1}) to the new chain in packets authenticated with the old chain, during a number of intervals before the end of the old chain, alternating between sending a disclosed key of the old chain and the commitment. The receiver keeps the commitment until the key K_{N+1} is disclosed, at interval N+1 plus the disclosure delay d, and can then test that key by computing F(K_{N+1}) and comparing it with the commitment. When the chain changes it becomes impossible to recover a previous key from the old chain, so if a receiver lost the packets disclosing the last key of the old chain the sender can re-send it for a number of additional intervals.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender starts from one random key and works backwards through a one-way function, so each key can only be checked against the one before it. One key is used per time interval. When the chain runs out the sender starts a new one and tells receivers in advance what its first key will hash to, so a forged commitment cannot be slipped in.

sections.title: What the Sender Adds to Each Packet
sections.content:
All the data packets sent must have an authentication tag containing the interval index i, which is also the index of the key used to compute the MAC of the packet; the MAC of the message, computed with K'_i = F'(K_i); and either a disclosed key, which belongs to the current or the previous key chain, or a commitment to a new key chain, or no key at all. The computation of the MAC must include the ALC or NORM header with its header extensions and the payload when applicable, and must not include the UDP and IP headers. During the computation the MAC field itself is set to zero.

The bootstrap information message and the direct time synchronization response message need to be signed by the sender. Both contain a Signature field, and the bootstrap message also carries the Signature Encoding Algorithm, the Signature Cryptographic Function and the Signature Length fields that let a receiver process the signature. The signature computation includes the ALC or NORM header and the payload, must not include the UDP and IP headers, and sets the Signature field and the optional Group MAC to zero, since the Group MAC is calculated later.

An optional Group MAC can be used to mitigate denial-of-service attacks from attackers who are not group members. It assumes a group key K_g shared by the sender and all receivers. When the attacker is not a group member, the benefits are threefold: a receiver can immediately drop faked packets without waiting for the disclosure delay; a sender can immediately drop faked direct time synchronization requests and avoid the computation-intensive check of a digital signature; and a receiver can immediately drop faked response and bootstrap messages without verifying a signature. The memo lists the limits too. It is no help if a group member who knows the key impersonates the sender, it requires an extra MAC computation per packet on both sides, and it makes the authentication headers larger. To limit that, the truncated MAC length n_w should be kept small, for example 32 bits, which means a forged packet has a one in 2 to the 32 chance of passing the check, and the memo argues this is acceptable because the Group MAC is only a pre-check followed by the standard TESLA check.
sections.plainLanguage: Every data packet carries the number of the time interval it belongs to and a short code computed with that interval's key. It may also carry the key itself, a promise about the next chain, or nothing. Some packets are signed with the sender's private key instead, because they set things up. An optional extra code lets receivers throw away most forgeries before doing any real work.

sections.title: What the Receiver Does
sections.content:
The verification of the authentication information must follow a strict order. First, if the Group MAC is present and the session uses the feature, the receiver verifies the Group MAC, and a packet without a Group MAC tag in a session that uses the feature must be dropped immediately, while a Group MAC tag in a session that does not use the feature must be ignored. Then it verifies the digital signature for the TESLA signalling packets, or enters the TESLA authentication process for data packets.

Authenticating an incoming data packet follows several steps. The receiver parses the headers, and if none of the four TESLA authentication tags are present it must discard the packet; in single key chain mode it must also discard any packet carrying a new key chain commitment or a last key of old chain disclosure. The safe packet test then records the local arrival time, computes an upper bound on the sender's clock at that moment, and works out the highest interval the sender could possibly be in. If that highest interval is less than the packet's interval index plus the disclosure delay, the sender is not yet in the interval during which it discloses the key, so the packet is safe but not necessarily authentic. If the test fails the packet is unsafe and must be discarded.

Next comes the Group MAC test, then the disclosed key processing. The receiver checks whether a legitimate key already exists with the same index, and if the values match it can skip the remaining key tests, while if they differ it must discard the packet. If the disclosed key index is new and no earlier legitimate key exists for the chain, the receiver ignores the disclosed key and skips the key verification test. Otherwise it checks the legitimacy of K_{i-d} by verifying, for some earlier disclosed and legitimate key K_v, that K_v and F applied i-d-v times to K_{i-d} are identical.

Only then can the MAC be recomputed and compared with the value carried in the packet, and the packet dropped immediately if the check fails. The memo notes that the receiver may discard unnecessary packets earlier, before the full set of checks is done, to save work.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver works in a fixed order. First it checks that the packet could not have been forged with a key that is not yet public, then it checks the cheap group code, then it checks the disclosed key against the chain it already trusts, and only at the end does it recompute the code on the packet itself.

sections.title: Integration in ALC and NORM
sections.content:
The integration of TESLA into ALC or NORM relies on the header extension mechanism defined in both protocols, and the memo details the EXT_AUTH header extension. Several fields are added to the Header Extension Type and Header Extension Length fields: an ASID field of 4 bits, which identifies the source authentication scheme or protocol in use, with the association between the ASID value and the actual scheme defined out of band at session startup; a Type field of 4 bits identifying the kind of TESLA information carried; and a Content field of variable length holding that information.

The Type values are 0 for bootstrap information, sent by the sender periodically or after a direct time synchronization request; 1 for a standard authentication tag for the ongoing key chain, sent along with a packet; 2 for an authentication tag without key disclosure, sent along with a packet; 3 for an authentication tag with a new key chain commitment, sent when approaching the end of a key chain; 4 for an authentication tag with a last key of old chain disclosure, sent some time after moving to a new key chain; 5 for a direct time synchronization request, sent by a NORM receiver; and 6 for a direct time synchronization response, sent by a NORM sender. The two time synchronization types are invalid in an ALC session, since ALC is restricted to unidirectional transmissions, although an external mechanism may provide the direct time synchronization functionality.

Each packet sent by the session's sender must contain exactly one TESLA EXT_AUTH header extension. All receivers must recognize EXT_AUTH but may not be able to parse its content, for instance because they do not support TESLA, in which case they must ignore the TESLA extensions. In the case of NORM, packets sent by receivers may contain a direct synchronization request but must not contain any of the other five TESLA header extensions. The bootstrap information header extension must be sent in a stand-alone control packet rather than in a packet containing application data, because of its large size, so that the maximum payload size of data packets is only affected by the mandatory authentication information header extension.
sections.plainLanguage: TESLA rides inside the header extension that ALC and NORM already have. One extension per packet, with a small type field saying what it holds, and the bootstrap message sent on its own so it does not eat into the space for content.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The general security of TESLA is discussed elsewhere and applies here. The memo draws out three points. Great care must be taken in the timing aspects, and in particular the parameter D_t, the upper bound on the lag of the receiver's clock with respect to the sender's, is critical and must be correctly initialized. If the sender realizes that the key disclosure schedule is not appropriate, the current session must be closed and a new one created, because the schedule parameters must be fixed for the whole session. And when the verifier that authenticates incoming packets and the application that uses the data are different components, there is a risk that an attacker between them injects faked data, and the same applies between the verifier and the secure timing system. For instance, if the verifier reads the local time with a dedicated system call and an attacker controls the host, the attacker may catch the call and return a faked time.

TESLA also introduces new opportunities for denial-of-service attacks. An attacker can try to saturate the receiver's processing capability, since faked packets are easy to create but checking them requires computing a MAC over the packet or sometimes checking a digital signature. An attacker can try to saturate the receiver's memory, since authentication is delayed and non-authenticated packets accumulate. An attacker can also make the receiver believe that congestion has happened, since congestion control must be performed before authenticating incoming packets. To mitigate these attacks the memo recommends the Group MAC scheme, and notes that no mitigation is possible if a group member acts as an attacker with the Group MAC. It also recommends that the amount of memory used to store incoming packets waiting to be authenticated be limited to a reasonable value.

Replay attacks, where an attacker stores a valid message and replays it later, have significant impacts that depend on the message type, and the memo separates the impacts within TESLA itself from the impacts within the ALC or NORM protocol. It also discusses the security of the back channel.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things matter most. The clocks have to be close enough that the delay bound is right, or the whole scheme can be fooled. And an attacker can still flood the receiver with junk that has to be checked and stored before it can be thrown away.

viz.caption: THE PIECES OF THE TESLA KEY CHAIN

items.title: Primary key K_N
items.text: A random key at the end of the chain. Its randomness is what makes the chain secure.

items.title: One-way function F
items.text: F(k) = f_k(0). The chain steps down with K_{i-1} = F(K_i).

items.title: Key derivation F'
items.text: F'(k) = f_k(1). The MAC key is derived from the chain key as K'_i = F'(K_i).

items.title: Chain length N
items.text: There are N+1 keys, one per interval, covering at most (N+1) times the interval duration.

items.title: Disclosure delay d
items.text: The number of intervals between a key being used and that key being revealed.

items.title: Committing to a new chain
items.text: The sender reveals the hash of the next chain's first key before switching, so a false commitment cannot be slipped in.

viz.caption: DIRECT TIME SYNCHRONIZATION, WHICH THE CHECKS DEPEND ON

messages.label: TIME SYNC REQUEST
messages.note: Carries the receiver's local time at the moment of sending.

messages.label: TIME SYNC RESPONSE
messages.note: Carries the receiver's time and the sender's time, and is signed.

messages.label: D_t COMPUTED
messages.note: The receiver derives the upper bound on the clock lag from the two times and a drift estimate.

viz.caption: THE VALUES OF THE EXT_AUTH TYPE FIELD

items.label: Bootstrap information
items.desc: Sent by the sender periodically or after a direct time synchronization request.

items.label: Standard Authentication Tag
items.desc: For the ongoing key chain, sent along with a packet.

items.label: Authentication Tag with a New Key Chain Commitment
items.desc: Sent when approaching the end of a key chain.

items.label: Authentication Tag with a Last Key of Old Chain Disclosure
items.desc: Sent some time after moving to a new key chain.

items.label: Direct Time Synchronization Request
items.desc: Sent by a NORM receiver; invalid in an ALC session.

items.label: Direct Time Synchronization Response
items.desc: Sent by a NORM sender; invalid in an ALC session.
